papers.title: Robustness of Skyrmion-Mediated Magnetization Switching in Perpendicular Magnetic Tunnel Junctions (p-MTJs) to Material Disorder and Elevated Temperature
papers.summary: Transient-skyrmion mediated voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy (VCMA) switching is a fast and energy efficient way to magnetization reversal, but its reliability under realistic material disorder and thermal fluctuations remain unclear. In this work, we use stochastic micromagnetic simulations of a 100 nm perpendicular magnetic tunnel junction to study switching reliability under grain-scale variations in Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, easy-axis orientation, and intergrain exchange coupling. We find that switching remains robust under moderate disorder, with 100% switching observed in 10^4 stochastic simulations after pulse width optimization at both 300 K and 350 K. Increasing the temperature from 300 to 350 K shifts the optimum VCMA pulse width from ~475 to ~450 ps, indicating that an apparent reduction in switching probability at a fixed pulse duration can be primarily due to pulse detuning. In contrast, strong easy-axis disorder reduces the maximum switching probability even after pulse-width optimization, indicating degradation of the switching dynamics. We further show that, under strong easy-axis disorder a transient skyrmion still forms while the subsequent post-pulse dynamics fails to complete the magnetization reversal. Our study therefore establishes the distinction between recoverable reliability due to timing shifts and permanent disorder-induced degradation that simply cannot be recovered by pulse re-tuning. Finally, for no disorders but at room temperature, 100% switching is observed with 10^6 stochastic simulations with correct pulse shaping.

papers.title: Vacancy-enhanced Li solid-solution anodes for solid-state batteries: computational screening enabling high critical current density
papers.summary: Sluggish vacancy-mediated self-diffusion in lithium metal limits the critical current density (CCD) of Li anodes in solid-state batteries by promoting interfacial void formation during stripping. To enhance the effective vacancy concentration while preserving the bcc Li host, we screen 50 substitutional solutes using density functional theory (DFT) within a funnel based on automatic phase diagram construction, solution energies, solute-vacancy binding energies, and experimental solubility limits. Using an adaptation of the Lomer model for the dilute limit, we show that only Ag, Ge, and Cd solid solutions are predicted to reach $1~\mathrm{mA~cm^{-2}}$ within their solubility limits. The thermodynamically estimated CCD of Ag at $\sim 9$ at.% reaches $\sim 4~\mathrm{mA~cm^{-2}}$ at a theoretical capacity of $1522~\mathrm{mAh~g^{-1}}$. Migration barrier calculations indicate that the enhancement may be partially offset by vacancy trapping, necessitating further validation via molecular dynamics simulations. Notably, Hume-Rothery rules alone prove insufficient as prefilters, whereas machine-learning models trained on the DFT data can eliminate most unsuitable solutes early in the funnel and extend the workflow to related solid-solution searches.

papers.title: Generating entanglement in quantum matter with pathway-entangled photons via resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
papers.summary: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) is conventionally used to probe elementary excitations and correlations in quantum materials. Here, we propose an interferometric RIXS protocol that instead creates entanglement between spatially separated regions of a solid-state material. An incident X-ray photon is coherently split by a beam splitter into two arms illuminating opposite ends of a sample. Recombining the scattered photons at a second beam splitter and detecting an energy-selected photon then projects the material into a coherent superposition of excitations at the two ends. This protocol is the X-ray, solid-state analogue of the Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller (DLCZ) heralding scheme. Using a Kramers-Heisenberg formalism with quantized photon modes, we show that orthogonal and degenerate end excitations yield maximally entangled states. We illustrate this mechanism in three models: (1) two decoupled sites yield a heralded Bell state. (2) An open tight-binding chain exhibits reflection-parity-dependent interference, providing a benchmark for the interferometer's coherence. (3) A spin-1 Haldane (AKLT) chain yields an entangled pair of fractionalized edge spins. We also discuss practical considerations and challenges for realizing the protocol in X-ray experiments.

papers.title: Extended Hydrodynamics of Planar Heisenberg Ferromagnetic Systems
papers.summary: Access to hydro and quasi-hydro regimes in magnetic systems is steadily increasing with the advances in fabrication of clean materials, and motivates study of hydrodynamics beyond conventional regimes and probe non-equilibrium transport. We employ the framework of extended irreversible thermodynamics which includes dynamical dissipative currents as quasi-hydro variables, and effect the modified hydrodynamic equations suitable to describe planar Heisenberg ferromagnetic systems in both paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. We show that the new transport coefficients and relaxation time scales introduced by quasi-hydro variables can engineer diverse combination of dispersion relations and provide control over the nature of hydrodynamic modes. For instance, we can change the diffusive energy mode into propagating one in multiple ways, including by tuning the relaxation time of magnetization current.

papers.title: CO2-Induced Shifts in the Confined Phase Transformation of CH4 in Metal-Organic Frameworks
papers.summary: A sharp increase in gas uptake over a narrow pressure range can occur for fluids confined in nanoporous materials such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), reflecting a transformation between distinct adsorption states, often accompanied by the existence of metastable states. Understanding how co-adsorbed species modify this behavior is important for predicting and optimizing gas storage and separation. Here, we investigate the effect of CO2 on the adsorption transformation of confined CH4 in rigid IRMOF-1 and IRMOF-8. Transition-Matrix Monte Carlo (TMMC) simulations were performed for systems containing 0-75 and 0-150 CO2 molecules in IRMOF-1 and IRMOF-8, respectively. While the addition of CO2 decreases the maximum CH4 uptake, consistent with competition for pore space, remarkably, the presence of CO2 significantly shifts the discontinuity in the CH4 adsorption isotherm to substantially lower pressures relative to the pure CH4 system. This promotion of the high-density CH4 phase at lower pressures demonstrates that CO2 substantially alters the thermodynamic landscape governing confined CH4 through changes in both fluid-fluid and fluid-framework interactions. These results establish CO2 as a thermodynamic modifier of confined CH4 behavior and suggest that controlled co-adsorption provides a means of tuning adsorption transformations in nanoporous materials.

papers.title: Combining Simulations and Spectroscopy to Design Protective Coatings on Sulfide Solid Electrolytes
papers.summary: Sulfide solid electrolytes are attractive for all-solid-state batteries because of their high Li-ion conductivity and favorable processability, but their practical use is limited by electrochemical instability and moisture-induced degradation. Molecular surface coatings offer a scalable strategy to improve humidity tolerance and interfacial stability, yet there is limited understanding of the molecular-level factors governing surface interactions. By combining large-scale atomistic simulations enabled by a machine-learning potential with targeted experiments, we present a comprehensive framework for designing molecular coatings on Li$_6$PS$_5$Cl (LPSCl). Using a PET-MAD interatomic potential fine-tuned on an r$^2$SCAN reference dataset covering LPSCl surfaces, molecular adsorbates, and their interactions, we model surface adsorption of carboxylic (CA), sulfonic (SA), and phosphonic (PA) acids with alkyl chains of varying lengths and the interaction of these coated surfaces with water at finite temperature. The simulations show that lithiated head groups generally exhibit more favorable adsorption energies. Impedance spectroscopy shows that the lithiated coatings maintain 40--55\% of the initial ionic conductivity after powder processing. While adsorption strength is largely controlled by head-group chemistry and lithiation state, coating morphology depends primarily on alkyl-chain length and surface coverage. In particular, long-chain lithiated carboxylates form dense, brush-like hydrophobic layers that reduce water access to reactive Li surface sites, with protection setting in at a coating thickness of approximately 0.8 nm. Consistent with these predictions, longer carboxylate chains suppress H$_2$S evolution more effectively. Because thicker coatings also hinder Li-ion transport, intermediate chain lengths offer the best balance between moisture protection and ionic conductivity.

papers.title: Rationalizing charge transfer: a single-molecule case study across three distinct surfaces
papers.summary: Organic molecules are versatile building blocks for the formation of complex low-dimensional nanostructures on surfaces. Recently, interest has grown in translating on-surface synthetic protocols from noble metal surfaces to insulating surfaces, which offer technological relevance, and to magnetic or superconducting surfaces, which offer new routes to correlated phases. It is important, therefore, to understand how these alternative surfaces may alter the properties of adsorbates through processes like charge transfer and screening. Evidence for charge transfer is often obtained experimentally via scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS), and theoretically via density functional theory (DFT). In this work, we systematically compare the properties of isolated macrocyclic emeraldine (Me$_6$) molecules on three different surfaces: metallic Au(111), a semiconducting ferromagnetic monolayer of FeCl$_2$, and a cleaved superconducting surface of bulk 2H-NbSe$_2$. We show that STS and DFT alone are insufficient to quantify charge transfer for these cases. Instead, we complement these methods with Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) measurements and model Hamiltonian calculations to demonstrate that on Au(111) and FeCl$_2$, Me$_6$ molecules donate a single electron to the substrate, whereas on NbSe$_2$ two electrons are transferred from molecule to substrate. Our work provides insight into the interplay of charge transfer, screening, and molecule-substrate coupling, and develops experimental and theoretical methods for comparing the properties of adsorbates across different surfaces for future studies.

papers.title: Configuration-Independent Low-Energy Gaps in Graphene Nanoribbons: A $δ$-Scatterer Transfer-Matrix Approach
papers.summary: Transport measurements on lithographically patterned graphene nanoribbons suggest that the gap depends primarily on ribbon width rather than on crystallographic edge orientation, in contrast to predictions of ideal tight-binding models. To address this, we develop a transfer-matrix approach, based on the theory of finite periodic systems, in which each carbon atom of the honeycomb lattice is represented by an individual $δ$-scatterer with interaction strength $γ^{}_δ$ and the nanoribbon is treated as a confined multichannel finite periodic system. We derive the unit-cell transfer matrix for both arm-chair and zig-zag edge configurations and obtain the transmission and channel-coupling coefficients in closed form. The transmission spectra display the resonant band structure characteristic of finite periodic systems, with the number of resonances per allowed band increasing with the number of unit cells. For $γ_δ=0$ the ribbons are fully transparent; for $γ_δ>0$ a low-energy transport gap opens and grows linearly with the scatterer strength, $Δ=0.364265\,γ_δ$, identically for arm-chair and zig-zag edges. These results are consistent with the reported absence of a systematic dependence on orientation, while the analytical results show that interchannel coupling vanishes exactly for arm-chair ribbons and decreases with increasing width for zig-zag ribbons, revealing the role of edge geometry. Together, these findings indicate that atomic-scale scattering, represented by the $δ$-potential formalism, provides a common orientation-independent contribution to the low-energy transport gap in the pristine ribbons considered here.

papers.title: Non-singlets and the phase diagram of Matrix Quantum Mechanics
papers.summary: The quantum mechanics of one $N\times N$ Hermitian matrix in the infinite $N$ limit is well known to define a two-dimensional string theory when the quartic coupling constant $g$ is tuned to a special negative value $g_*$. We study the thermodynamics of this Matrix Quantum Mechanics (MQM), treating the SU$(N)$ symmetry as a global symmetry. Crucially, the non-singlets, i.e. states in non-trivial representations of SU$(N)$, implement the effects of vortices on the discretized worldsheets. This random lattice model has the low-temperature $c=1$ and high-temperature $c=0$ phases, with the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition separating them. We map out the phase diagram in the coupling--temperature plane, which is separated by the critical stability curve $T_c(g)$ extending from $g_*< g <0$. We study this curve using the non-perturbative matrix bootstrap and low- and high-temperature perturbation theory, which explain the thermal instability. At low temperatures, thermally excited non-singlets backreact on the Fermi sea of matrix eigenvalues, causing it to spill over. At high temperatures, the theory is described by an effective matrix integral obtained by dimensional reduction on the thermal circle; the eigenvalue distribution of the zero mode becomes unstable at the critical coupling. We conjecture that the BKT transition occurs at a special point on the critical curve and estimate its position. Finally, we switch to the regular square lattice and study the MQM-inspired Villain model, where the link factor is the one-dimensional propagator on a circle. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we map out the BKT transition in this model.

papers.title: Magnons and excitons from Bethe-Salpeter equation and its application to graphene-based magnets
papers.summary: With the recent isolation of two-dimensional semiconducting magnetic materials, the theoretical study of spin-flip collective excitations (magnons) along with spin-conserving electron-hole bound pairs (excitons) has become particularly relevant. Describing both types of quasiparticles within the same theoretical framework is possible, in principle, but the well-established many-body formalism for the calculation of excitons, based on the intertwined Bethe-Salpeter and Hedin's equations, is not satisfactory for magnons, since the usual approximations produce a spurious gapped Goldstone mode. Here, we show that excitons and magnons can be computed on the same footing under the same Bethe-Salpeter formalism, while respecting the gapless Goldstone mode for magnons. We demonstrate how this can be achieved through the evaluation of the full Bethe-Salpeter equation, beyond the Tamm-Dancoff approximation in model Hamiltonians. As an example, we apply it to ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic graphene, faithfully represented by the extended Hubbard model. Our results clarify the roles of on-site and non-local interactions in exciton and magnon appearance and identify consistency requirements relevant to extending the approach to first-principles calculations.

papers.title: Finite-Temperature Transconductance of Multiterminal Josephson Junctions with Topological Andreev Spectra
papers.summary: Multiterminal Josephson junctions (MTJJs) provide a controllable platform for engineering topological Andreev spectra. At zero temperature, Andreev bound states (ABSs) with nonzero Chern numbers give rise to quantized transconductance between superconducting terminals. We derive the finite-temperature transconductance of MTJJs using linear-response theory. We first demonstrate the destructive role of temperature: changes in the thermal occupations of the ABSs destroy exact transconductance quantization. We then show that finite temperature can also play a constructive role by making the transconductance sensitive to finite-energy topological crossings hidden from the zero-temperature response. Our results establish the thermal limitations of transconductance quantization and identify finite-temperature transport as a probe of otherwise inaccessible topology in Andreev spectra.

papers.title: Unconventional charge density wave order in ErTe$_{3}$: symmetry breakings and fluctuations probed by Raman scattering
papers.summary: Recent experiments have revealed unexpected mirror-symmetry breakings in the charge density-wave (CDW) state of rare-earth tritellurides, suggesting a putative ferro-axial CDW state. Here we report polarization-resolved Raman scattering measurements tracking the point-group symmetry breakings across the CDW phase transition in the rare-earth tritelluride ErTe$_3$. We show that the mirror-symmetry breakings follow closely the emergence of the CDW order, suggesting a single component CDW order parameter. Furthermore, Raman measurements in the $A_{2g}$ symmetry channel above the CDW transition temperature indicate the absence of significant ferro-axial fluctuations. We discuss the broad implications of these findings with respect to the nature of the CDW state in the tritellurides.

papers.title: Ginzburg-Landau Theory with Elastic Incompatibility Describes the Liquid-G-phase-Crystal State Diagram
papers.summary: We derive a mechanically consistent Ginzburg-Landau theory for the metastable heterogeneous G state reported in deeply undercooled metallic liquids. The central result is that type-II-like mixed-state physics can emerge structurally with the random internal stress field playing the role of the magnetic field. Frozen eigenstrain due to elastic incompatibility between ordered cores and the amorphous matrix generates incompatible stress, while the non-affine internal strain in the liquid-like matrix in between the ordered cores relaxes that stress over a finite screening length $λ_σ$ (analogous to the London length in the superconducting problem). Structural order heals over a distinct mechanically-dressed length $ξ_G$; their ratio $κ_G=λ_σ/ξ_G$ provides the structural counterpart of the Ginzburg-Landau parameter. Because the matrix is transiently rigid yet locally relaxational only over an intermediate time window, the same mechanism selects crystal for slow protocols, a heterogeneous G state at intermediate rates, and a homogeneous L-like glass under rapid arrest. Residual incompatibility frustrates coarsening, allowing finite ordered cores and screened, orientation-dependent core interactions. The resulting texture is an inverted Abrikosov analogue: structural order resides in the cores, whereas incompatible-stress screening is carried by the surrounding disordered matrix. The theory yields direct simulation and experimental tests through stress-decay, structural-healing, non-affine-susceptibility, and kinetic measurements.

papers.title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
papers.summary: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $α=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $α/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $α_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.

papers.title: Majorana Edge-to-bound State Transition in Interferometric Superconductor Rings
papers.summary: Manipulating flux quanta in topological superconductors is central to vortex braiding in quantum computing. Their interferometric superconducting rings can host either topologically protected edge states with fluxes confined inside the central hollow area or vortex bound states in flux cores at the annulus walls. Here we demonstrate a strategy to drive topological edge states into vortex bound states by tuning the relative scale of vortex size and annulus width in nano-ring interferometric device on 2M-WS$_2$ topological superconductor. Near its superconducting transition where the coherence length exceeds the annulus width, Little-Parks oscillations exhibit expected periods for flux bundles in ring-center, consistent with edge states residing at inner and outer rims of the annulus. Upon cooling, where the coherence length shrinks below the annulus width, the unexpectedly increased oscillation period reflects multiple fluxes distributed along annulus region in flux necklace configuration, implying a transition from extended edge states to localized vortex bound states. Ginzburg-Landau simulations and local density-of-states calculations with Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations reveal that large values for both Ginzburg-Landau parameter and flux-pinning energy are vital for such a transition. Our findings provide a novel strategy for understanding flux manipulation towards flux braiding and topological quantum computing.

papers.title: Floquet Engineering of Momentum Gaps in Magnonic Time Crystals: Slow-Drive Amplification and In-Gap Propagation
papers.summary: Photonic time crystals host momentum gaps in which waves grow exponentially but cannot propagate. We establish their magnonic counterpart in a thin film with periodically switched anisotropy, deriving its Floquet band structure and confirming it micromagnetically. Gaps require a precession-ellipticity contrast. The waveform controls high-order gaps: a single 1~GHz switching drive amplifies a comb of spin-wave bands, from 2.5 to 4.5~GHz, above Gilbert losses even with smoothed edges, unlike sinusoidal modulation. With the Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya interaction, amplified packets propagate inside the gap while growing.

papers.title: Spontaneous Decay of High Energy Composite Fermions
papers.summary: An electron, when added to a fractional quantum Hall fluid, famously splits into fractionally charged composite-fermion quasiparticles. We show here that a high energy composite fermion carrying a fractional charge decays into a collection of particles, including quasiparticles, quasiholes, and even whole electrons.

papers.title: Tensor Networks for Materials Simulation and Quantum Chemistry
papers.summary: Predicting the properties of correlated materials and molecules often requires a many-body description that goes beyond single-particle and mean-field approximations. Tensor networks address this challenge by exploiting the entanglement structure of quantum states to construct compact, systematically improvable representations. Although developed largely for idealized model Hamiltonians, these methods are increasingly being integrated into material-specific calculations. This Perspective introduces their underlying principles and examines how network geometry, bond-dimension truncation, and approximate contraction determine the accuracy and computational reach of these approaches. We survey applications across regimes of increasing complexity, ranging from ground-state properties of quantum magnets and itinerant-fermion systems to excitation spectra, nonequilibrium dynamics, finite-temperature and open systems, and molecular electronic structure. We then examine four routes connecting these methods to real materials, including experimentally constrained models, downfolded Hamiltonians, dynamical mean-field theory with tensor network impurity solvers, and quantum embedding. Throughout, we evaluate the maturity of existing capabilities and their principal limitations, synthesizing this assessment into a practical method-selection guide. We argue that reliable materials predictions require quantifying uncertainties introduced at each stage, from constructing material-specific Hamiltonians to extracting experimentally accessible observables. Finally, we identify the algorithmic advances and reproducible computational practices needed to establish tensor networks as a routine tool for predictive materials science and quantum chemistry.

papers.title: First- and Second-Order Electron Position Correlators Reveal Topological Phase Transitions
papers.summary: The theory of conventional critical phenomena is built around the concepts of fluctuations and correlators of local observables. Here, we show that topological phase transitions can also be characterized through spatial and temporal two-point correlation functions associated with fluctuations of the electronic position operator. The key object is the antisymmetric part of the position-position correlation function, which yields the Chern number in the equal-time and equal-space limit. When the system is translationally invariant in space or time (the latter case corresponding to an equilibrium condition), these two-point correlators reduce to one-variable functions of the remaining variable. Remarkably, these functions are both reminiscent of critical behaviour, including divergent correlation times and lengths signalling the phase transitions. Away from these conditions, namely in non-periodic systems or genuinely dynamical processes, criticality is instead better captured by higher-order Chern-Chern correlators constructed from local or dynamical markers obtained as coincident-point limits of the position correlators. These higher-order Chern-Chern correlators can be seen as double Levi-Civita contractions of second-order position correlators, selecting the antisymmetric sector in each index pair. We substantiate this framework through numerical simulations and analytic calculations. Our results establish a general correlator-based description of topological phase transitions, applicable to crystalline, noncrystalline, equilibrium, and dynamical systems.

papers.title: Entanglement Asymmetry and Asymmetry Contour under Boundary Symmetry Breaking
papers.summary: We investigate how symmetry-breaking boundary magnetic fields affect magnetization and Rényi-2 entanglement asymmetry (EA) in the transverse-field Ising model. For the ground state, magnetization exhibits qualitatively distinct behaviors in the ordered and disordered phases. EA also exhibits phase-dependent behavior, which is well captured by the lower and upper bounds derived in this work. In the critical regime, both magnetization and EA exhibit behavior qualitatively consistent with the field-theoretical predictions for a related setup. We also study boundary-quench dynamics and find that magnetization propagates from the boundary into the bulk with a velocity consistent with the maximum quasiparticle velocity. In contrast, because EA is a subsystem-integrated quantity, its spatial structure is not directly resolved. We therefore introduce the asymmetry contour, a contour-like finite-difference quantity that provides a spatially resolved characterization of the symmetry-breaking information encoded in the reduced density matrix. The resulting contour is complementary to the local magnetization, retaining sensitivity to nonlocal many-body correlations while its dynamics also reflects the underlying quasiparticle propagation. These results show how EA and its contour can provide complementary information-theoretic characterizations of symmetry breaking and its spatial structure.

papers.title: Controlled Fabrication of Uniform Columnar Porous GaN Architectures by Electrochemical Etching
papers.summary: Electrochemical etching (ECE) of n-type c-plane GaN enables the formation of porous architectures capable of enhancing the performance of optoelectronic devices and broadening the range of possible GaN applications. Here, we demonstrate that the addition of NaOH to Na2C2O4 (and other non-acidic etchant solutions) directs ECE toward the formation of nanoscale, vertically aligned, highly uniform columnar pore morphologies with relatively limited surface roughening. By varying the NaOH concentration within mixed electrolyte systems, the columnar pore shape, diameter, spacing, and bulk and surface porosity can be readily tuned. In addition to manually mixing NaOH with another etchant, aqueous basic electrolytes such as Na2CO3 and Na3PO4, each inherently containing significant hydroxide concentration through hydrolysis, also produce similar columnar pore morphologies, indicating that hydroxide plays the key role in directing the vertical pore growth. Chronoamperometry and pore structure analysis reveals that the mixed hydroxide-containing electrolyte systems exhibit a distinct, new ECE mechanism rather than a simple superposition of the individual ECE behaviour of each anion present. This work provides significant insight into the ECE mechanism for porous GaN, which is proposed to contain multiple reaction steps where hydroxide anions are involved in the formation of a reactive intermediate. These findings establish a versatile and controllable route for engineering columnar porous GaN architectures, offering significant advancement in applications requiring high porosity, ordered, and bespoke structures.

papers.title: Nano-ARPES observation of a flat band at the \bar{M} point in 2.4° twisted bilayer graphene
papers.summary: The emergence of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at the so-called magic angle reveals a range of intriguing phases, such as superconductivity and Mott insulating states, resulting from electrons entering a correlated state. This establishes twisted bilayer graphene as an excellent platform for exploring correlation effects in many-body phases and across various twist angles. However, in most cases, the twist angle is not an easy parameter to control because it exhibits structural instabilities such as relaxation and reconstruction that reduce the correlation effects. Here, we report the unexpected appearance of a flat band at the \bar{M} point far from the Fermi level in a 2.4° twisted bilayer graphene, directly visualized by angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Our work is the first observation of flat bands away from the \bar{K} point in twisted bilayer graphene and highlights the need to probe the entire Brillouin zone to fully capture electronic states in twisted structures.

papers.title: On the Spontaneous Structural Reconstructions of Chalcogen-Depleted MoS$_2$, MoSe$_2$, and Janus MoSSe Monolayers
papers.summary: Removing one chalcogen layer from a transition-metal dichalcogenide monolayer leaves an undercoordinated sheet that reconstructs as the remaining chalcogen atoms cross the metal plane. Here, we combine \textit{ab initio} and reactive molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of depleted MoS$_2$, MoSe$_2$, and Janus MoSSe, examining each remaining chalcogen on two parent lattices, to show that the remaining chalcogen type determines the structural reconstruction, with only a minor influence from the parent lattice. In \textit{ab initio} trajectories of the Janus-derived sheets, Se crosses the Mo plane already at 300~K, whereas S stays in place at 300~K and the sheet reconstructs only at 900~K. With a free in-plane cell, the crossings precede an anisotropic lattice contraction, which therefore results from the structural reconstruction. Reactive MD simulations of 50~nm sheets show that, when S remains, the Mo lattice stays crystalline in nanometric domains that disappear with time and temperature, with pores/holes at 900~K. In contrast, when Se remains, the Mo lattice loses crystalline order within the first picosecond, and 36--39\% of the Se atoms cross at every temperature. In a depleted lateral MoS$_2$/MoSe$_2$ heterostructure, both modes coexist in one sheet, each half reconstructing like its single-chalcogen counterpart, suggesting chalcogen patterning as a route to define crystalline and disordered regions in a single monolayer.

papers.title: Discrete WKB approach to density profiles in inhomogeneous two-band free-fermion chains
papers.summary: We extend the discrete WKB method to one-dimensional bipartite tight-binding chains of free fermions with slowly varying hopping amplitudes and on-site potentials. We focus on the inhomogeneous Rice-Mele model, suggesting possible experimental realizations thereof in optical superlattices. We derive explicit semiclassical expressions for the single-particle wave functions and density of states, as well as the sublattice-resolved local particle densities and filling fraction at arbitrary Fermi energy. In particular, we show that the WKB density profiles agree with those obtained from the local-density approximation. We analyze the spatial dependence of the local band edges and its consequences for the global spectral structure, and clarify the role played by the phase-space topology in determining the Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization conditions. Finally, we illustrate our results with two representative examples: a homogeneous Rice-Mele chain subject to a harmonic trap and a fully inhomogeneous chain containing a domain wall.

papers.title: Stochastic and quantum autonomous information machine: efficiency fluctuations, precision and optimization
papers.summary: We investigate the conversion between thermal and informational resources in an autonomous machine coupled to thermal reservoirs and a tape, playing the role of an information reservoir. The machine is able to perform information erasure driven by heat, and information-powered refrigeration, for which we introduce suitable efficiency definitions. We focus on the role of fluctuations in the currents and stochastic efficiencies, as well as in operation at optimal performance. The model is also extended to allow a coherent information reservoir, which is able to modify operation and performance. All in all, our work provides insights for the design and optimization of information-to-work conversion devices at small scales.

papers.title: Probing the limits of forward screening and inverse design of crystal materials
papers.summary: Crystal materials are designed either by screening known crystals for a target property or by generating new crystals with that property. Both routes are judged against public databases of known crystals, but these databases name the same crystal differently. Several materials announced as new by recent generative and autonomous discovery campaigns have since proved to be known phases or close variants of them. The limits of both routes remain unmeasured. Here we probe them by matching the crystals of 55 databases by structure into one self-extending database of 14.6 million crystals and 131.8 million property values, each traced to its source. Only 4.5% of its crystal-property pairs carry a value. To fill the empty pairs, we developed CGTNet, an equivariant graph transformer with state-of-the-art accuracy on several tasks of two public benchmarks. Trained on each task, it forms a library of property models whose predictions we release. The reach of forward screening has been underestimated. Known crystals hold tens of thousands of ultra-incompressible candidates without a recorded bulk modulus, and a post hoc audit of synthesis evidence finds among them ReN2, whose bulk modulus was measured at 428 GPa. The novelty claimed for inverse design has been overestimated. At an equal verification budget, a stiffness-conditioned generator returned more stiff hits than screening (100 versus 55), but all contained osmium and 82 repeated recorded compositions. Integrating and completing the databases of known crystals therefore moves the limits of both routes: it widens what screening can reach and sets the reference against which generated crystals are judged new.

papers.title: High-quality, deep formation and identification of oxygen-vacancy defects in silicon carbide
papers.summary: Optically addressable paramagnetic defects in silicon carbide (SiC) are attractive for scalable quantum technologies such as quantum sensing. PL5, PL6, and PL7 are promising defects for their high brightness and spin-readout contrast. Although generation by oxygen implantation has been reported very recently, nonuniform spin and optical properties and the limited generation depth of implanted defects hinder both high-sensitivity sensing and conclusive microscopic identification. Here we engineer high-quality defects by decoupling oxygen incorporation and defect formation, realizing highly homogeneous spin-resonance frequencies as well as narrow optical linewidths and long T2* coherence time. Further, we demonstrate defect formation beyond the ion range utilizing oxygen diffusion, exceptional among impurities in SiC. We further provide hyperfine-interaction statistics of 17O and host nuclei across many PL6 defects, making the oxygen-vacancy origin conclusive. Together, the microscopic identification and the demonstrated formation route establish a foundation for developing the oxygen-vacancy spin defect into a versatile quantum platform.

papers.title: QuantumBilliards.jl: An extensible, user friendly, high-performance Julia library for the large scale computation of spectra and eigenstates of quantum billiards and related problems
papers.summary: We present QuantumBilliards.jl, an open-source Julia library providing a suite of numerical solvers for the two-dimensional interior Helmholtz eigenproblem with Dirichlet boundary conditions, a paradigmatic model in quantum chaos. The library implements conventional wavenumber-sweep techniques together with several accelerated eigensolvers: the Vergini--Saraceno scaling method, the expanded boundary integral method (EBIM), Beyn's contour-integral method, and the Compact Rational Krylov (CORK) method. It provides a common framework for constructing billiard geometries, exploiting discrete symmetries, computing eigenvalues and eigenstates, and treating smooth, cornered, and multiply connected domains. The library further includes reconstruction of eigenfunctions from boundary normal derivatives and the computation of Poincaré--Husimi (PH) phase-space representations. Available at: https://github.com/Quantum-Chaos-Julia/QuantumBilliards.jl.

papers.title: Multi-scale patterns arising from competing chemotactic interactions
papers.summary: Classical chemotaxis models consider the directed motion of cells in response to a chemical gradient. Recent experiments suggest that biological microswimmers such as bacteria can perform chemotaxis toward multiple chemicals, which dynamically evolve depending on the distribution of the microswimmers. In this Letter, we consider a mass-conserving chemotaxis model in which pattern formation is driven by two competing chemicals, autoinducers and nutrients, where the former acts as an activator and the latter as an inhibitor for coarsening. We show that this can give rise to diverse patterns including long wavelength uninterrupted coarsening, Turing-like arrested coarsening, traveling waves as well as a novel class of mixed multi-scale oscillatory coarsening patterns, where a dense aggregate coexist with a dynamically spreading part of the population. We analytically derive the conditions for the onset of such patterns and discuss their physical implications, which significantly broadens our understanding of signaling active matter and pattern formation in general.

papers.title: Magnetic Anisotropy and Magnetization Dynamics in Si/Ni Multilayers Probed by FMR and VSM Magnetometry
papers.summary: The magnetic anisotropy and magnetization dynamics of sputtered [Si(40~Å)/Ni($t_{\mathrm{Ni}}$~Å)]$_{20}$ multilayers were systematically investigated at room temperature using SQUID--VSM magnetometry and angle-dependent ferromagnetic resonance (FMR). Static measurements reveal soft ferromagnetic behaviour in thicker Ni layers and mixed ferromagnetic and superparamagnetic contributions at reduced thicknesses. The saturation magnetization increases toward the bulk Ni value with increasing thickness, consistent with Ni nanocrystallite growth. Magnetic dead-layer analysis yields an interfacial dead-layer thickness of approximately $9$~Å per interface, accounting for the suppressed magnetization in thinner Ni layers. Angle-dependent FMR measurements reveal effective easy-plane magnetic anisotropy, while out-of-plane spectra exhibit additional non-uniform spin-wave modes. The effective magnetization remains lower than the static saturation magnetization, indicating a perpendicular anisotropy contribution that partially compensates the demagnetizing field. Quantitative anisotropy analysis yields an interfacial anisotropy constant of $K_S = +0.17~\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}}$, favouring perpendicular magnetization, and a volume anisotropy constant of $K_V = -1.23 \times 10^6~\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-3}}$, favouring in-plane alignment, with an extrapolated anisotropy crossover thickness of $t_c \approx 27$~Å. Increasing FMR line-shape asymmetry with decreasing Ni thickness is consistent with enhanced interfacial roughness. These findings highlight the competing interfacial and volume anisotropies and the importance of Ni thickness and interface quality in tailoring Si/Ni multilayers for silicon-compatible spintronic applications.

papers.title: Modification of optical properties in ultrathin ALD-grown NbN layers using oxygen plasma treatment
papers.summary: NbN thin films with a nominal thickness of 10 nm were grown by atomic layer deposition (ALD) on Al$_2$O$_3$-buffered Si substrates and treated with oxygen plasma for 0 s (untreated), 20 s, 40 s, and 60 s to investigate oxygen-induced changes in their optical properties. Spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) measurements were performed before and after oxygen plasma treatment over the ultraviolet-visible-near-infrared (1.24-6.20 eV) and infrared (0.041-0.827 eV) spectral ranges. Film thickness determined by X-ray reflectivity (XRR) was used as a fixed parameter in the optical modeling to extract the dielectric function, optical constants, and effective free-carrier concentration. We observed the emergence of a distinct absorption feature near 4.9 eV following oxygen plasma treatment, consistent with the oxidation of the NbN surface and the resulting change in its optical properties. Increasing the treatment time from 0 to 60 s reduced the effective carrier concentration from $1.20 \times 10^{22}$ to $1.03 \times 10^{22}$ cm$^{-3}$ and the effective carrier mobility from 2.44 to 2.27 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$. The obtained results provide a basis for understanding the effects of oxygen plasma treatment on NbN thin films.

papers.title: Excitonic Stark Response Induced by Quantum Capacitance in van der Waals Heterostructures
papers.summary: Precise electrostatic control in van der Waals heterostructures is commonly described by a geometric capacitor model, which assumes that the internal electric field is fully determined by external gate voltages. Here, we show that this description breaks down in the presence of interfacial charge transfer, where quantum capacitance modifies the internal electrostatics. Using interlayer excitons as local probes, we observe a dipole-dependent energy splitting that persists even when the gate-induced geometric field is nominally canceled. This splitting reflects incomplete cancellation between gate- and carrier-induced fields set by quantum capacitance, while many-body renormalization is largely symmetric with respect to the two opposite dipole orientations, allowing the splitting to provide a direct optical measure of the local chemical potential. Our results reveal the central role of quantum capacitance in interface electrostatics and provide a route to probe it in operando.

papers.title: Effect of oxygen plasma treatment on the structural and superconducting properties of atomic-layer-deposited NbN thin films
papers.summary: Surface oxidation is a common concern for ultrathin NbN superconducting devices, yet which superconducting properties it affects has not been established for films grown by plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition. We expose NbN films about 11.4 nm thick to an O$_2$ plasma for 0 to 60 s, which oxidizes the surface without etching the film, and characterize the same sample series by X-ray diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and transport measurements on 500 nm wide nanowires. XPS of the surface and the underlying layer shows that the plasma converts the surface to Nb$_2$O$_5$, whereas the bulk of the treated film is chemically identical to that of the untreated film. Crystalline $δ$-NbN remains intact. During exposure, the total film thickness rises and saturates between 40 and 60 s, indicating self-limiting surface oxide growth. The normal-state resistivity rises by 21% (dc) and 25% (optical) with the plasma dose, while the critical temperature and transition width are unchanged. The switching current densities of 4.9-6.2 MA/cm$^2$ at 4.2 K show no systematic dependence on the plasma dose. Their temperature dependence follows the dirty-limit depairing current of Kupriyanov and Lukichev, and the extrapolated switching currents reach 39-46% of the depairing current calculated from the optical resistivity and diffusion coefficient, in agreement with the width dependence reported for nanowires from the same process. The oxygen signature is confined to temperatures near $T_c$, where the supercurrent of the treated wires vanishes at least 0.5 K earlier than that of the untreated wire, consistent with a partially oxidized surface layer that acts on the film by the proximity effect. At these doses, oxygen narrows the temperature range of the supercurrent from above but does not systematically reduce the low-temperature current-carrying capacity of the wires.

papers.title: Divalent Yb in the Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ Structure Type: Crystal Growth and Physical Properties of Yb$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$
papers.summary: We report on the single-crystal growth, crystal structure, and physical properties of Yb$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$. Single crystal x-ray diffraction shows that the material crystallizes in the Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ structure-type at ambient conditions, described by orthorhombic symmetry $Pbam$. Magnetization measurements reveal a nearly isotropic diamagnetic response, indicating that Yb is stabilized in a non-magnetic divalent configuration. Electrical resistivity measurements show a metallic behavior. First-principles calculations including spin--orbit coupling describe a metal whose states at the Fermi level are dominated by Bi $6p$ orbitals, with a density of states within 1% of that of the isoelectronic compound Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$, consistent with a filled and chemically inert $4f$ shell. They further show that the nonsymmorphic symmetry of the crystal enforces fourfold-degenerate nodal lines on the Brillouin-zone boundary, four of which cross the Fermi level and give symmetry-enforced Dirac points with a linear transverse dispersion. Despite strong metallic and covalent bonding within the Pd-Bi network, Yb$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ is realized as a rare-earth analog of the Ca$_3$Pd$_4$Bi$_8$ structure type with divalent Yb ions. This result offers a potential avenue to discover other rare-earth analogs within this structural family.

papers.title: Hybrid Monte Carlo for the extended Kane-Mele-Hubbard model
papers.summary: The Hubbard model offers a powerful minimal description of strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials, yet it neglects effects observed in nature that give rise to a much richer variety of physics. For instance, including nonlocal interactions introduces a competition between strongly correlated phases, while incorporating spin-orbit coupling (SOC) can lead to the emergence of exotic topological phases. Seeking a more realistic platform for simulating graphene and, potentially, related materials such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), we therefore consider the extended Kane-Mele-Hubbard model, which features a Kane-Mele SOC term and nearest-neighbor interactions. Simulating this model is particularly challenging once the nonlocal interactions become dominant over the on-site Hubbard interaction, as a severe sign problem arises already at half filling, leaving this regime largely unexplored. In this work, we develop continuous auxiliary field formulations of the model, suitable for treatment with the Hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) algorithm. Using these formulations, we characterize the sign problem across the model's parameter space and establish where simulations are feasible, as a first step toward the full phase diagram.

papers.title: Multifractal Magnons Around Localized Defects
papers.summary: Multifractal wavefunctions fluctuate over a hierarchy of spatial scales, remaining spatially extended while exhibiting strongly nonuniform structure. We show that magnons in otherwise crystalline two-dimensional magnets can exhibit such behavior on mesoscopic scales, without disorder or quasiperiodicity. A localized defect can mix discrete groups of nearly degenerate magnon states in a finite sample, generating multiscale interference patterns and multifractal wavefunctions. We demonstrate this mechanism for both a simple spin defect and topological magnetic skyrmions. Large-scale spin-wave calculations for skyrmions in chiral and frustrated magnets reveal clear multifractal diagnostics over the full accessible range of system sizes of above-gap modes. Crucially, skyrmions make these states experimentally observable by hybridizing them with magnetically active internal deformation modes, which gives a subset of the multifractal states a nonzero magnetic dipole moment. These states can therefore be excited by uniform ac fields and remain distinguishable at realistic frequency resolution, providing a direct route to observing mesoscopic magnon multifractality.

papers.title: Side-Chain Engineering Controls Molecular Packing and Vertical Electron Transport in Discrete n-Type NDI-T2 Oligomers
papers.summary: High-efficiency vertical charge transport in multilayer organic optoelectronic devices highly depends on molecular structure and arrangement. Using two T2-(NDI-T2)2 conjugated oligomers with ethylhexyl (EH) and octyldodecyl (OD) side chains as a model system, their effects on electron transport are investigated using, among other techniques, atomic force microscopy (AFM), conductive atomic force microscopy (C-AFM), grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS), steady-state optical spectroscopy, and time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) calculations. The oligomers of both materials exhibit relatively disordered structures in the as-cast state, whereas annealing enhances structural order and leads to side-chain-dependent changes in molecular stacking. EH-based films show a smaller annealing-induced photoluminescence shift than OD-based films, suggesting less pronounced stacking and conformational rearrangements, consistent with TDDFT-supported exciton analysis. The current-voltage characteristics are analyzed using the space-charge-limited current (SCLC) model. After annealing, both materials exhibit improved vertical electron mobility. The EH-based films reach a maximum mobility of 1.2 x 10^-4 cm^2 V^-1 s^-1. The combined results suggest that the shorter EH side chains modify the out-of-plane packing environment and facilitate vertical electron transport. These results establish a structure-property relationship between side-chain structure, molecular order, exciton coupling and vertical mobility, providing a molecular design basis for optimising organic semiconductors through side-chain engineering.

papers.title: Interplay of Chemical Disorder, Vortex Pinning, and Electron Correlations in the Mechanically Robust Medium-Entropy Alloy Superconductor $\text{Nb}_{0.45}\text{Ta}_{0.25}\text{Ti}_{0.15}\text{Hf}_{0.15}$
papers.summary: Medium and high-entropy alloys have emerged as a promising class of superconducting materials because their intrinsic chemical disorder can simultaneously enhance mechanical robustness and modify superconducting properties. Here, we present a combined experimental and first-principles investigation of the structural, superconducting, electronic, and local lattice-distortion characteristics of the mechanically robust medium-entropy alloy $\text{Nb}_{0.45}\text{Ta}_{0.25}\text{Ti}_{0.15}\text{Hf}_{0.15}$. The material shows type-II superconductivity with a transition temperature $T_C^{onset} \approx 7.8 ~\mathrm{K}$. A high critical current density of $J_c = 0.48 \times 10^{6}~\mathrm{A/cm^2}$ is observed, and this is attributed to strong vortex pinning at grain boundaries. Specific-heat analysis indicates a strong electron-phonon coupling ($λ$ = 1.07) with a large isotropic s-wave superconducting gap. Density functional theory calculations explicitly model the intrinsic chemical disorder, predict a stable body-centered cubic phase. These calculations further reveal a metallic electronic structure with substantial Ti- and Ta-derived states at the Fermi level. Additionally, our results quantify a pronounced disorder-induced local lattice distortion ($Δd = 0.086$ A), providing a microscopic basis for the experimentally observed enhanced vortex-pinning landscape. Remarkably, the alloy also exhibits an unusually large Kadowaki-Woods ratio, placing it close to the heavy-fermion regime and indicating enhanced electronic correlations beyond conventional alloy superconductors. Our results demonstrate that entropy-engineered chemical disorder can stabilize robust superconductivity, promote strong flux pinning, and induce correlated electronic behavior, establishing refractory medium-entropy alloys as a promising platform for next-generation superconducting materials.

papers.title: On the Role of Atomic Mobility in the Polyamorphism of Metallic Glasses
papers.summary: Understanding the microscopic mechanisms underlying polyamorphic transitions requires simultaneous knowledge of thermodynamic and structural evolution, which has remained experimentally inaccessible. Here, we combine chip-based fast differential scanning calorimetry with high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction to simultaneously probe the thermodynamic and structural evolution during the polyamorphic transition of a Pd-Ni-P metallic glass. Correlating heat-flow signals with the corresponding structural evolution during both heating and cooling reveals a direct relationship between thermodynamic evolution and medium-range structural ordering. Based on this relationship, we identify two distinct transition mechanisms. In the glassy state, the transition proceeds continuously through progressive medium-range ordering, accompanied by enhanced thermal stability and strongly temperature-dependent kinetics. In contrast, in the equilibrium supercooled liquid, the transition proceeds through the coexistence of distinct amorphous states, with only a weak temperature dependence of the kinetics. These findings show that atomic mobility governs the transformation pathway by coupling thermodynamic evolution to structural ordering, providing new insights into polyamorphic transitions in nonequilibrium amorphous systems.

papers.title: Compression of turbulent flow data through an extended space-time correlation: certification against the modal energy budget
papers.summary: The fidelity of direct numerical simulation now outpaces the storage and data-movement capacity available for the resulting fields. We present an open, distributed, GPU-accelerated low-rank compression framework for large turbulent flow databases. We assess it using two direct numerical simulations of a controlled diffusion compressor cascade under laminar and turbulent inflow conditions. Compression is formulated using a correlation operator over space and time, which is two orders of magnitude larger than that of snapshot POD. Its dominant range is extracted with a randomized range finder based on communication-avoiding hierarchical QR. The compressed databases are evaluated through a hierarchy of increasingly strict diagnostics, from instantaneous reconstruction and second-order statistics to the modal turbulent kinetic energy budget and its nonlinear interscale transfer. The budget terms are far more sensitive to compression than fieldwise or one-point errors. They remain accurate at conservative compression and degrade sharply once the retained energy is relaxed. The near-wall dissipation and the interscale transfer degrade the most and set the admissible compression level. An aggressive reduction preserves every one-point statistic to within a few per cent while corrupting both by an order of magnitude more. The dissipation error is confined to the viscous sublayer and grows with the development of the boundary layer. It is carried by the high-order modes. For both inflows, the linear budget terms scale with the discarded energy to the power $0.8$ and the triadic transfer to a power above one.

papers.title: Electron Wavefronts Capture Nanoscale Movies of Hypersound at Surfaces
papers.summary: Acoustic waves transport mechanical energy and elastic strain through solids, with material composition and shape governing their propagation. In the gigahertz hypersound regime, acoustic wavelengths reach tens to hundreds of nanometres, comparable to nanoscale device dimensions. Harnessing these waves underpins high-frequency signal processing, sensing, electromagnetic coupling and quantum control. Acoustic metrology probes elastic modes and internal interfaces. Yet directly imaging how nanoscale acoustic waves interact with local structure remains challenging, requiring picometre displacement sensitivity combined with high spatiotemporal resolution. Here we demonstrate full-field imaging of laser-induced hypersound at surfaces using reflected electron wavefronts. We introduce ultrafast low-energy electron microscopy (ULEEM), exploiting the intrinsic surface sensitivity of few-electronvolt electrons. Coherent electron pulses down to femtosecond durations reflect from the topmost atomic layers, imprinting the evolving surface profile onto their wavefronts. Defocus converts phase variations into image contrast. In a thin van der Waals material, we image the thermoelastic generation and propagation of picometre-amplitude acoustic waves. Measured dispersion relations, interpreted through elastodynamic modelling, distinguish substrate-supported and locally detached regions, revealing how interfacial contact shapes propagation. Delayed wave emission reveals scattering at buried mechanical defects. Our results establish electron-wavefront imaging of nanoscale surface dynamics, enabling the exploration of ultrafast energy transport, structural transformations and coupled mechanical, electronic and magnetic phenomena.

papers.title: Quantum Landau Lifshitz Gilbert equation in ferromagnetic conductors and magnetic insulators
papers.summary: Understanding the microscopic origin of magnetic damping is essential for describing magnetization dynamics in nanoscale magnetic systems. In this work, we develop a microscopic framework to derive Gilbert damping terms from specific interactions in ferromagnetic conductors and magnetic insulators. In ferromagnetic conductors, magnetic damping is dominated by the s d exchange interaction between the localized magnetic moments and the itinerant electrons, which is effectively equivalent to an electronmagnon interaction. From the spin diffusion equation and the spin transfer torque therein, we obtain the corresponding quantum LLG equation. In magnetic insulators, where free electrons are absent, spin phonon interactions become the primary source of the damping.Starting from an effective spin phonon interaction and using linear response theory, we derive a quantum LLG equation with a Gilbert damping tensor analytically. Our results demonstrate that different microscopic interactions lead to qualitatively different structures of magnetic damping. Instead of being described by a universal scalar parameter, Gilbert damping can exhibit spatial dependence and tensorial characteristics determined by the underlying microscopic interactions.

papers.title: Integrable turbulence and statistical properties of chaotic wave fields in the complex modified Korteweg-de Vries equation
papers.summary: This paper investigates integrable turbulence and the mechanism for generating rogue waves in the complex modified Korteweg--de Vries (mKdV) equation through numerical simulations and statistical analysis. We solve the Lax pair eigenvalue problem using the Fourier collocation method and establish a correspondence among solitons, breathers, and rogue waves on the spectral plane. We generate chaotic wave fields by simulating the complex mKdV equation using the split-step Fourier method, starting from a plane wave with superimposed random noise. We analyze the effects of the standard deviation \(μ\) and the correlation length \(L_c\). The results show that increasing \(μ\) drives a transition from breather turbulence to soliton turbulence, increasing the probability of rogue-wave generation.In contrast, \(L_c\) primarily influences the spatial scale of the structures. As the constant background of the complex mKdV equation is modulationally stable, its integrable turbulence does not depend on modulational instability. Compared with the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation under identical initial conditions, the complex mKdV equation attains comparable amplitudes under strong perturbations, but exhibits a higher spatial gradient. This suggests that third-order dispersion and derivative nonlinearity alter the excitation mechanism and steepen the waveform.

papers.title: Low-Temperature Hybrid Monte Carlo for Perylene and Corannulene: Stabilizing Determinant and Force
papers.summary: We demonstrate a real world physics study of the molecules perylene and corannulene at different doping levels, and calculating selected one-, two- (exciton) and three-body (trion) correlators. This has been done by performing Hubbard-model simulations near room temperature. We find, between charge neutral and doubly charged plateaus of perylene, an interaction-induced $ΔQ = 1$ plateau whose width grows with interaction strength and in which the ground state is a spin doublet rather than a singlet. The algorithmic advancement enabling this study simultaneously stabilizes the determinant and force calculations to machine precision at room temperature, while scaling as well as standard determinant Quantum Monte Carlo simulations of these systems. Furthermore, our formalism retains the full time-displaced (2-point) Green's function, allowing us to construct any $n$-body correlator, including those that contain disconnected diagrams.

papers.title: Strain-tunable van Hove singularity and superconducting dome in monolayer kagome metal CsTi$_3$Bi$_5$
papers.summary: The recently discovered titanium-based kagome metal CsTi$_3$Bi$_5$, which exhibits superconductivity without an accompanying charge density wave, provides an ideal platform to investigate the intrinsic electronic structure and superconductivity. Moreover, it enables the exploration of superconductivity in the two-dimensional limit of the kagome lattice. Here, we systematically investigate the influence of biaxial mechanical strain ($\varepsilon$) on the electronic structure and superconductivity of monolayer CsTi$_3$Bi$_5$ using first-principles calculations. We demonstrate that the prominent van Hove singularity (VHS) at the M point can be monotonically tuned to the Fermi level by tensile strain. Furthermore, the superconducting transition temperature $T_C$ exhibits a dome-shaped dependence on strain, reaching a maximum of 3.6 K at an optimal tensile strain of $\varepsilon=+2\%$. The average superconducting gap magnitude is 0.35 meV, with an orbital-dependent and anisotropic distribution. Our results provide a detailed understanding of the superconductivity of monolayer CsTi$_3$Bi$_5$ and show that strain is an effective, continuous tuning knob for manipulating the electronic structure and superconductivity.

papers.title: Flexo-Photoresponses from First Principles
papers.summary: Many functionally important materials, such as silicon, possess high-symmetry crystal structures that forbid even-order nonlinear optical responses, thereby limiting their application in e.g., photonics and optoelectronics. Strain gradients can effectively break symmetries, activating otherwise forbidden optical responses. Although such flexo-photoresponses have attracted considerable interest recently, a comprehensive microscopic theoretical framework is still lacking. Here, we develop a first-principles approach that can systematically evaluate a wide range of flexo-photoresponses in realistic materials. By mapping strain gradients to long-wavelength phonons within the established theory of electron-phonon coupling, our approach captures the nonlocal quantum-mechanical effects of lattice deformations on nonlinear optical responses. Applying the framework to prototypical centrosymmetric materials, including Si, cubic $\rm SrTiO_3$, and monolayer black phosphorus, we demonstrate that a strain gradients of $10^5\sim10^6~\rm m^{-1}$ can induce flexo-second-harmonic generation and flexo-bulk photovoltaic effects comparable to the intrinsic responses of non-centrosymmetric crystals. Our work establishes a rigorous foundation for strain gradient engineering of light-matter interactions, opening new avenues for nanoscale optomechanics, optoelectronics, and beyond.

papers.title: CoPiT: A conditional Position-induced Transformer for aerodynamic field prediction on unstructured meshes
papers.summary: High-fidelity Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) simulations remain a standard tool for aerodynamic analysis, yet each solve on an unstructured mesh is computationally expensive, making many-query tasks such as design exploration, optimization, and multi-condition evaluation costly. Neural operators provide mesh-flexible surrogates for mapping geometry and operating conditions to flow fields; however, in many existing architectures, global parameters such as the freestream state and design variables are concatenated with pointwise inputs, leaving their influence on intermediate features implicit. This paper proposes CoPiT, a \textbf{Co}nditional \textbf{P}osition-induced \textbf{T}ransformer that builds on the Position-induced Transformer (PiT) as its geometric backbone and injects a global condition vector through multi-stage feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), thereby making parametric modulation explicit while preserving geometry-based attention weights. The model is evaluated on two-dimensional AirfRANS airfoil fields, including scarce-data and extrapolation regimes, and on three-dimensional BlendedNet++ blended-wing-body surfaces. On the AirfRANS full-data test set, CoPiT reduces surface and volume losses by approximately 54\% and 24\% relative to Transolver, respectively, and achieves the lowest overall normalized test MSE among the compared baselines on BlendedNet++. Matched ablations show that FiLM conditioning generally improves upon input concatenation, while the preferred placement is task-dependent. CoPiT thus provides a practical operator-learning surrogate for parametric aerodynamics on unstructured meshes.

papers.title: Banded Chaos and Time-Semicrystalline Order
papers.summary: Recent work has introduced the notion of a time semicrystal, a driven nonequilibrium regime in which subharmonic temporal order survives inside deterministic chaos. Here we revisit this phenomenology from the viewpoint of classical nonlinear dynamics. Banded chaotic attractors consist of a finite number of chaotic sectors cyclically permuted by stroboscopic evolution, allowing discrete subharmonic spectral components to coexist with a broadband chaotic continuum. Exemplified through the driven Duffing oscillator and the logistic map, this structure naturally reproduces the characteristic signatures of time-semicrystalline dynamics. Within this framework, periodic subharmonic motion can enter chaos through the familiar period-doubling cascade while retaining a well-defined temporal skeleton governed by the universal Feigenbaum scaling. Temporal order within chaos can also reorganize or collapse through distinct mechanisms, producing continuous or abrupt transitions that may be intertwined with symmetry changes. These results connect time-semicrystal phenomenology with established structures of dissipative nonlinear dynamics, showing that its essential ingredients already arise in standard nonlinear systems and providing a simple framework for extending and testing the paradigm in more complex, many-body, and experimental settings.

papers.title: Near-field maps of topological edge states of molecular aggregates
papers.summary: Self-assembled two-dimensional molecular aggregates provide a versatile platform for engineering excitonic states, including topologically nontrivial edge states. However, these edge-states are difficult to probe optically: they have weak far-field transition strengths, and far-field spectra do not reveal whether an excitation is localized at the edge. For an aggregate consisting of two sublattices of molecules with genuinely complex transition dipoles, we show that spatially resolved near-field spectroscopy encodes the full spatial structure of these states. The resulting near-field maps do not mirror the site populations, but instead exhibit strongly nonuniform, interference-like features. We demonstrate that a convolutional neural network can reconstruct the complex expansion coefficients of the eigenstates from these maps, and that this reconstruction is robust against substantial random noise.

papers.title: Triplon dynamics from partial Kondo screening in frustrated heavy-fermion systems
papers.summary: The partially disordered (PD) phase, in which magnetically ordered and Kondo-screened sites coexist, has been proposed as a possible ground state of geometrically frustrated heavy-fermion systems. We investigate its dynamical properties in the half-filled periodic Anderson model on a triangular lattice by calculating the dynamical spin susceptibility within the random-phase approximation built on a self-consistent Hartree-Fock solution. We show that successive quantum phase transitions from the Kondo-insulating phase to the PD phase and to a magnetically ordered phase are driven by the condensation of triplon modes originating predominantly from the Kondo-screened sites. In the PD phase, magnons and triplons coexist and hybridize, leading to characteristic level repulsion in the excitation spectrum. These results reveal how triplet excitations evolve into collective magnetic modes across the successive phase transitions and highlight the dynamical interplay between magnetic order and Kondo screening in frustrated heavy-fermion systems.
